claims.text: Mechanical loading under demanding service conditions induces stress-driven elemental segregation at grain boundaries in the initially single-phase HEA.
Stress-driven grain-boundary segregation locally destabilizes the single-phase solid solution.
Local destabilization produces nanoscale brittle intermetallic or ordered clusters.
The nanoscale clusters act as crack-nucleation sites and accelerate brittle fracture.
The initial HEA is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution with an equiaxed microstructure and random elemental distribution.
Fatigue or slow-strain-rate loading promotes diffusion-driven segregation.
Mechanical deformation enhances atomic mobility at stress concentrations, particularly at grain boundaries.
Enhanced atomic mobility drives elemental segregation and local compositional fluctuations.
Segregation and local compositional fluctuations reduce grain-boundary cohesion.
Segregation encourages the nucleation and growth of brittle secondary phases.
Brittle grain-boundary secondary phases facilitate intergranular cracking during continued mechanical loading.
Mechanically pre-loaded specimens will have lower fracture toughness than the as-processed baseline.
Mechanically pre-loaded specimens will exhibit a greater tendency toward brittle intergranular fracture than the baseline.
Mechanically pre-loaded specimens will exhibit nanoscale segregated or ordered phases along grain boundaries detectable by TEM/EDS or APT.
The proposed mechanism applies at approximately 300–600 K when sustained or cyclic loading permits significant stress-assisted atomic mobility.
The mechanism does not apply where stress and temperature are insufficient to induce measurable segregation.
Environmental hydrogen effects and other alternative embrittlement mechanisms are excluded from the proposed mechanism.
